About: The Bohr Atom — Energies Crowd In, Orbits Spread Out

Source

Topic
Atomic structure — the Bohr model of hydrogen-like atoms
Concept
As n grows the energy levels crowd toward zero while the orbits fly apart as n² — the two run in opposite directions.
Audience
JEE / NCERT Class 11–12
Misconception targeted
"Higher energy means further out AND more energetic, so everything grows together" — the energy does rise (toward 0), but the gaps between levels SHRINK.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A charge going in circles

One electron circles a proton, held there by the Coulomb attraction. Circular motion is acceleration, and classical electromagnetism says an accelerating charge radiates energy continuously.

The left panel shows orbit radii; the right panel shows the electron's energy, measured down from E = 0, the energy of an electron just barely free of the atom.

2 · The classical prediction

The orbiting electron radiates energy away continuously. On classical physics alone, what becomes of this atom?

3 · Bohr's postulates

Bohr kept only the orbits whose angular momentum is a whole multiple of h/2π, so that m vₙ rₙ = n h/2π, and declared that an electron sitting in one of them does not radiate at all.

Those orbits are the rings on the left and the rungs on the right — the sidebar's m vₙ rₙ / ħ reads exactly n. Radiation appears only when the electron jumps from one rung to another.

4 · From n = 2 to n = 4

Raising n from 2 to 4 makes the orbit radius four times larger. By what factor does the energy gap to the next rung up change?

5 · A nucleus of charge +2e

Swap the proton for a helium nucleus of charge +2e, with the electron still at n = 1. Its energy deepens from −13.6 eV to −54.4 eV. What happens to the orbit radius?

One electron circles a nucleus of charge +Ze, and the sim draws two views of the same atom side by side. The left view shows the orbits, and the right view shows the energy of each orbit.

What you'll learn

  • How the radius and the energy of a Bohr level depend on n and on Z.
  • How the energy gap between neighbouring levels depends on n.
  • What the m v r / ħ line in the panel checks.

03

Classical physics predicts a collapse

An electron circling a proton is always accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. Classical electromagnetism says an accelerating charge radiates energy, so the electron should lose energy and spiral inward.

Integrating the radiated (Larmor) power inward from r = a₀ gives a collapse time

t = a₀³ / (4 rₑ² c) ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹¹ s
rₑ = 2.82 × 10⁻¹⁵ m is the classical electron radius, a₀ = 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

The emitted frequency would also sweep up smoothly as the orbit tightens, so there would be no sharp spectral lines. Real atoms last indefinitely and give sharp lines.

See itSelect n = 1 for hydrogen. Watch for: rₙ / a₀ = 1.00 and a speed of 2.188 × 10⁶ m/s, the starting orbit of that estimate.
04

Bohr allows only orbits with m v r = nħ

Bohr kept only orbits whose angular momentum is a whole multiple of ħ = h/2π. He declared that an electron in such an orbit does not radiate. Radiation happens only in a jump between two allowed orbits.

m v r = nħ   (n = 1, 2, 3, …)

Newton's law for the Coulomb force, m v²/r = Z k e²/r² with k = 1/(4πε₀), fixes v for each r. Combining it with the postulate gives the radii

rₙ = n² a₀ / Z

The sim finds v from Newton and Coulomb alone, so the m v r / ħ line in the panel is a check on the postulate. It reads n for every orbit.

See itSelect n = 3 for hydrogen. Watch for: m v r / ħ = 3.00 and rₙ / a₀ = 9.00 in the panel.
05

Energy levels crowd together as n grows

With kinetic energy ½mv² = Zke²/2r and potential energy −Zke²/r, the total is Eₙ = −Zke²/2rₙ, which gives

Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV

Zero is an electron just free of the atom, so the ground state of hydrogen, −13.6 eV, takes 13.6 eV to ionise. The gap from n to n + 1 is

ΔE = 13.6 Z² (1/n² − 1/(n+1)²) eV

For hydrogen, ΔE is 1.890 eV at n = 2 and 0.306 eV at n = 4. The radius grows by a factor of 4 over the same step while the gap falls by a factor of 6.2.

See itSelect n = 4 for hydrogen. Watch for: gap to n + 1 = 0.306 eV and the Δ label on a ladder whose upper rungs bunch together.
06

A larger Z pulls the electron closer and binds it harder

Z enters the two formulas with different powers: rₙ = n²a₀/Z falls as 1/Z, while Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² deepens as Z². The speed follows vₙ = 2.19 × 10⁶ × Z/n m/s.

The sim's Z = 2 is He⁺, a helium nucleus with one electron. At n = 1 its radius is 0.265 Å and its energy is −54.4 eV, so it takes 54.4 eV to remove that electron.

At Z = 4 (Be³⁺) the ground-state speed is 8.75 × 10⁶ m/s, about 3 % of c. This model describes one-electron ions only, which is why Z stops at 4.

See itSelect n = 1 and change Z from 1 to 2. Watch for: the rings contracting, r = 0.265 Å and E = −54.423 eV in the panel.
07

Photons come from jumps between levels

When the electron drops from level nᵢ to a lower level n_f, the atom emits a photon carrying the energy difference:

hν = 13.6 Z² (1/n_f² − 1/nᵢ²) eV

For hydrogen, the jump 3 → 2 gives 1.890 eV. With hc = 1240 eV nm, that is a wavelength of 656 nm, the red Balmer line. This is the same number as the n = 2 gap in the panel, since adjacent rungs are one jump apart.

Jumps down to n = 2 from ever higher levels approach 3.40 eV, or 365 nm, because the rungs bunch up. The sim shows rungs and gaps, not photons.

See itSelect n = 2 for hydrogen. Watch for: Δ = 1.89 eV between the n = 2 and n = 3 rungs, the 3 → 2 photon energy.
08

Where it matters

  • Hydrogen spectrum. The Lyman (ultraviolet), Balmer (visible) and Paschen (infrared) series all follow hν = 13.6 (1/n_f² − 1/nᵢ²) eV. The Lyman line for 2 → 1 is 10.2 eV, or 121.5 nm.
  • One-electron ions. He⁺, Li²⁺ and Be³⁺ obey the same formulas, with their lines pushed to higher energy by Z².
  • Ionisation energy. The 13.6 eV for hydrogen and 54.4 eV for He⁺ are the values the panel shows as the energy to free the electron.
Go deeper

Bohr's levels match hydrogen's energies well, but electrons do not travel on orbits. In quantum mechanics the ground-state electron is a probability cloud, and a₀ is its most probable radius. The model also fails for atoms with two or more electrons.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim pairs the orbits of a one-electron atom with its energy levels, for a chosen n and nuclear charge Z.

Key points

  • Classically the orbiting electron would radiate and collapse in about 10⁻¹¹ s.
  • Bohr's rule m v r = nħ gives rₙ = n²a₀/Z and Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.
  • Radii grow as n² while the gaps between levels shrink.
  • A jump's photon carries the energy difference of two levels.

Common mix-ups

  • "A bigger orbit means a bigger energy gap." The orbits spread out as n², but the gaps between levels shrink.
  • "The orbiting electron radiates, so Bohr's atom must too." In Bohr's model it does not. Radiation comes only from jumps.
  • "A larger Z changes only the energy." It shrinks the radius by 1/Z and deepens the energy by Z².

Things to try on your own

  • Step n from 1 to 6 at Z = 1 and write down the gap to n + 1 each time.
  • Find another setting with E = −13.606 eV, the same as n = 1, Z = 1.
  • Find another setting with r = 0.529 Å, the same as n = 1, Z = 1.
